video_title: An honest conversation about what's happening in AI
transcript: Today, I’m joined by Ege  Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo.  Ege is a researcher at Google DeepMind. Daniel is one of the authors at the AI Futures   Project, which published AI 2027 and AI 2040. I wouldn’t call this exactly a debate,   because I hope it’ll be more of a discussion. But there is a set of key disagreements you   guys have, which leads one of you, Daniel,  to believe that AI is likely to kill us all   within the next few years, and Ege,  you to believe that will not happen.  I feel like a big crux in this  conversation is just timelines.  How soon do you expect extreme superintelligence? I’ve articulated, and Paul has articulated in   the last episode, why there could  be extreme superintelligence soon.  Ege, why do you think that’s unlikely? The main difference between me and Daniel,   and also between me and Paul, is just how much  you believe in the software-only singularity.  This is the idea that you have a fixed  pool of compute and a roughly fixed   amount of data that is at least not synthetic. Then what happens is that you get better AIs.  Those AIs are able to use that pool of  resources way more efficiently to make   progress on AI research, and you get this  feedback loop that at least goes for many   orders of magnitude before it fizzles out. Then that improvement is so big that you get,   I don’t know, 10 years of progress in six  months or whatever, something like this.  I think the evidence we have is not  sufficient to give high credence to that.  Maybe that’s 10-20% likely to  happen over the next three years.  That’s probably the biggest disagreement,  where Daniel thinks that’s over 50% likely.  Why do you think it’s more than 50% likely  that there will be extreme superintelligence   within the next few years, whereas  Ege thinks that’s 10-20% likely?  First of all, I don’t think that we will  probably all be dead in a couple years.  The thing I would say is, unless we substantially  slow down the AI companies, then probably we will   lose control and there will be misaligned  AIs running the show in a couple years.  It seems like we’re getting close to  fully automating the AI research process.  That would be the main claim. How close? It seems like   it’s going to happen in 2027. Maybe not, maybe 2028, maybe 2029, but I would   say it’s slightly more likely than not in 2027. Once you have fully automated the AI research   process, things will probably accelerate. More likely than not, they will accelerate a lot,   as Ege was describing, although I do  think there’s some uncertainty there.  Then I think that a lot of the limitations of  current AI systems, such as the data inefficiency   or whatever, will melt away relatively  quickly as progress accelerates dramatically.  You’ll end up with AIs that are able to flexibly  learn quickly from all sorts of experience.  You might call them  top-expert-dominating AIs, perhaps.  Top-expert-dominating AIs are effectively  superintelligence as far as I’m concerned.  Here’s a naive question. We go back five  years and we have AI systems that can’t   even hold a conversation. Now we have systems that   are solving Millennium Prize Problems. They’re pretty good coders, et cetera.  If we just go another five years of  progress at this pace, do you think   it’s likely that that alone gives us AIs  that are competitive with human experts?  If we’re looking forward five years,  do we even need that much RSI?  We might not, but I think it’s unclear. If we don’t get any RSI, my median timeline   to everything being automated and humans having  nothing to do — they’ve been completely automated   — is something like 15-20 years from now. That’s a median timeline. So in the next   five years, you still have to give it  20% or something that it could happen.  I think that’s a very live possibility. While there are disagreements about software-only   singularity and similar things, in some sense  those disagreements don’t matter that much.  All I’m saying is, Daniel is saying something is  50-60% likely to happen over the next three years,   and I’m saying it’s 20% likely. That question might be interesting.  But even if it’s only 20% likely,  if the situation is very bad,   you should still do something about it. So even though it’s maybe a larger   disagreement numerically, I don’t think it’s  a significant disagreement qualitatively.  So the reason why you’re working at Google  instead of protesting outside of Anthropic,   which is a practical difference between our  behavior, is less to do with the probabilities   on the different scenarios and more to do  with… Well, what actually? I’m curious.  Several things. In this particular question  of whether a pause is a good idea or not,   I’m worried about any plan that involves us acting  on risks before we have seen some significant   version of the costs in the real world. Right now, the thing people always cite   in these discussions, since some number of  months ago, is the Hugging Face incident.  But I personally think the Hugging Face incident  didn’t cost that much and was a pretty small   incident in the grand scheme of things. It was much less significant than a plane   crash in terms of the cost imposed. I do see it as analogous to if you   have a new technology, like nuclear  reactors or aircraft or whatever,   and you haven’t actually seen anything significant  go wrong, but you have all these theoretical   arguments for why things might go wrong, and  you’re intervening on the basis of that… I’m   just suspicious about that approach in general. The thing I’m challenging when I say that is   the view that the way you get aligned AIs is to  have some theoretical breakthrough in alignment.  Nothing in machine learning has worked like that. Machine learning is not a field that has   large theoretical breakthroughs. There have been no large theoretical   breakthroughs over the past 10 years. All of them have been incremental.  You stack this compute multiplier  on top of this compute multiplier,   and you get this efficiency gain. It’s just very incremental. There are a   lot of dimensions that you optimize at once. That’s the way you make them more capable.  So I don’t see why you would  assume anything different   about the way we would make them more aligned. This is maybe a key disagreement between you guys.  Are there tractable  interventions that we could make?  Specifically, are those interventions  more tractable if we get more time to   make them, interventions that are likely  to increase the value of what these AI   systems do and how they treat us? The AI Futures Project has just   put out a pacing scheme that you say  will delay the intelligence explosion   by a year, which you are expecting in 2027. So you think this would slow it down to 2028?  Something like that. We  have uncertainty, but yeah.  What changes if we get the intelligence  explosion in 2028 rather than 2027?  A couple things. First of all, I think  that progress is being made on AI alignment   and the science of understanding how AI  works and all sorts of things like this.  It’s not going fast enough, but it is being made. Each additional year of time that we buy, there’s   additional progress, which cuts away at that  probability mass of the bad outcomes happening.  The second thing I would say is just  general awareness, what you might   call AGI-pilling of society and of government. This might actually be the most important thing.  Most people just don’t really take this  stuff seriously, don’t really understand   what’s happening or what’s coming. That seems broadly bad to me.  We’d probably be in a better situation if more  people in general understood what was coming.  I think that process is happening. It might even be happening exponentially.  Every year that goes by, more people  learn more, more people pay attention,   more people start getting involved. It’s just very difficult without   tangible things that the technology does in  the world to wake people up to its potential.  For example, if we pause at the current level  of capabilities, let’s assume we do that.  Yes, this process of people  waking up continues slowly.  But just look at the skepticism in the financial  markets about the viability of this technology.  There’s huge skepticism. That’s also probably  just shared broadly throughout the public.  The public doesn’t really like AI. They don’t really like data centers and stuff.  But that’s not because they  realize what’s going to happen.  They just have a much more myopic distaste for it. If we pause now, then people are still not going   to understand what’s at stake. The public conversation about   this will still be very poor because  it will be operating from bad premises.  There’s an advantage to getting the  capabilities to a point where it’s   evident to everyone that if we keep going from  there on, the world will be totally transformed.  Because doing this through ordinary  persuasion is extremely difficult.  You might get some kind of pause politically,  but it would be supported by factions who   don’t actually agree with your worldview. They would support it for some other reason.  They don’t like big tech companies. They don’t like the fact that all these companies   are constructing all these data centers that  the local communities they’re in don’t support.  It would be for some other reason and not for  the reason that you think is most important.  I technically agree with  you, but in spirit disagree.  Maybe one way of modeling it is something like:  for each new AI capability that appears, there are   some rapid updates that people make immediately  just upon learning that that capability exists.  But then there’s a whole bunch of additional  updates that get made as that capability gets   more deployed into the world and so forth. Right now capability progress is moving fast   enough that we still haven’t nearly exhausted  the gains in awareness that would come from   just deploying the current capabilities more. If we had a pause where we continue to deploy the   current capabilities but not make them smarter,  we would continue to see significant gains in   awareness over the course of several years. Then it would taper off after more than that.  I do think that things are going fast  enough now that to a first approximation,   the wake-up is a function of serial time  rather than a function of the capabilities.  Although there’s some  function of the capabilities.  Another thing I would say too is that a lot of  the people who have anti-AI opinions don’t share   my worldview and don’t have anti-AI  opinions for the same reasons as me.  But that’s also changing to a larger extent.  We’ve seen multiple senators and congresspeople  come out and say, "AI could kill us all," and,   "The AIs could go rogue," and things like that. That’s mostly happened just in the last year.  So that too is trending in what I  would consider the right direction,   where people are waking up and understanding  the magnitude of the situation more.  I don’t think it’s trending fast  enough in the right direction.  I don’t think that it’s going to be  where it needs to be in 12 months,   but in 24 months maybe, or in 36 months maybe. I agree with the point that if you pause now,   you will still get an increase in  awareness for a couple more years.  But given the distance between where we are  now and where I think people need to get,   given the implications of technology, I think  that’s just not going to happen if you pause   at the current level of capabilities. It might be enough. You might have the   view that the current level of support  and current political coalitions or   whatever are sufficient to get a pause to happen. Then that has the benefits that you care about,   that it slows things down, even though it’s not  done with a complete understanding of what’s going   to happen and it’s done for different motivations. It’s a defensible position. I’m just worried   in the longer term that if we as a civilization  just insist on being irrational about this topic,   then we will just make a lot of bad choices, a  lot of choices that don’t make that much sense.  It’s important that people understand that  in some ways, the world we’ve been in is   going to no longer exist in some sense. Even if the outcome is very good for us,   if you get Daniel’s ideal outcome or  something like that, that world is   still completely different from today’s world. People don’t realize. Maybe if they realize,   they’ll be like, "Wait, we don’t want that world. That doesn’t fit our preference.  We want some other world." But if there is never an explicit   conversation that has the correct factual premises  about what’s going to happen, then we will just   not be in control of the situation. Because even though in some sense we   are in control, in the sense that all the  relevant decisions, at least for a while,   are being made by humans, they are not being  made as a result of some rational deliberation.  I’m really worried about that. Some random thing is going to happen,   and we won’t control what happens. It will not be the output of any   process that makes any sense. Then we will have to live with it.  That’s very scary. That’s a reason to go slower in AI development.  It’s a reason to go slower after sufficiently many  people are aware of the potential of technology.  And you think it’s too early for that? I think it’s too early.  Then what about, instead of going  to a complete pause, going slower?  Say we do the thing where we restrict AI R&D  compute to 10% or 5% of the company’s compute.  This slashes the overall pace of progress  by a factor of two or three or something.  Perhaps you would agree then that because you are  still making forward progress, you are still going   to get the levels of awareness eventually. A couple things about that.  First of all, I don’t know how to get  international coordination for this.  Given what we’re currently doing, it’s  going to be very hard because the US   is being quite adversarial against China  right now, especially with recent events.  That just seriously undermines the  possibility of getting any coordination.  It’s actually very myopic and dangerous. They really have to stop doing that.  One of the nice things about the  10% idea is that it would still   leave the US companies with about as much  compute on AI R&D as the Chinese companies.  Also, because a lot of Chinese progress  is just coming from the US, you wouldn’t   even need a deal to do this level of pacing. For now, but that’s because China is behind on   a bunch of the industrial tech that’s  required to produce a lot of compute.  For example, they don’t have access  to EUV machines and stuff like this.  The US has been able to get the Netherlands to  successfully export control those and so on.  But given China’s rate of economic  growth and industrial progress,   these are temporary advantages. So it gives us some time.  China is not going to be able to  catch up in five years, probably.  So if you think five years is enough, then you  can get five years with a method like this.  But if you think we need 15 years or something  like that, then I become more pessimistic.  Or let alone some global agreement. In the limit, it is worth discussing.  If you really believe we’ll have such powerful  AI systems, this depends on what you think the   nature of destructive technologies is. But it is plausible that you might need   some global treaty on, "Hey, you can’t have  superintelligent systems that you’ve deployed   to go research mirror life or something." At some point, there’s not just a race.  Unless you think you’re just going to  literally outcompete every single country.  I agree that ultimately, if we want to have a  good future, we’re probably going to need to   make some sort of treaty or deal with China  and other countries, something like that.  If you’re really worried about that risk,  there has to be coordination with them.  There’s no way to avoid that. You can try to delay things.  You can have a five-year lead. You have five additional years.  That buys you something. But if  you’re really worried about that risk,   they could try to build it in five years. It’s not that long. Any prospects of coordination   with them, I think, are being severely damaged by  the policy of the US government towards China, and   also, to some extent, of Anthropic towards China. I agree with that.  This is very short-sighted. It’s because people  don’t understand the stakes of the technology.  The awareness that this is a world-transforming  technology that completely changes the condition   of civilization is just not there. We have to figure out a way to deal   with it, and there’s no way to adequately deal  with it without some kind of coordination.  And people are torpedoing the prospects for doing  that for some very short-sighted, short-term gain   of, "Oh, we get a couple years’ additional lead." It doesn’t make sense, what people are doing.  So I think they’re operating from a very different  view of what the technology will be like,   which I think is going to have bad consequences. This is another thing I think is not being   discussed, even in communities where people  are trying to think of, "How do we win?  How do we get the safe AI first?" Gwern had an interesting comment about this,   I think on LessWrong, where he asked  the question: let’s say the US wins.  We get our superintelligence. Then  what? What do we do? Do we do some   crazy operation to try to overthrow the  Chinese government or something like that?  If they think that’s what the US is going to do,  what are they going to think of any attempt to try   to coordinate with them to get a slowdown? They’re inherently going to be extremely   suspicious of any such attempt  if they think that is the plan.  Even if you don't know my sponsor, WorkOS,  you've probably used their products.  That's because a bunch of companies  like Anthropic, OpenAI, Plaid, Granola,   and Wispr Flow rely on them behind the scenes to  power things like authentication and permissions.  WorkOS has spent the better part of the last  decade building these features for human users.  And now they've taken that expertise and applied  it to agents, building products that let agents   log in, grab the right permissions,  and take actions within your product.  Take Agent Auth. You start by defining  permissions for the most powerful agents   that you'd be comfortable with. Now, not every agent will actually   get these permissions. This is just your ceiling.  Then, whenever a user kicks off an agent in your  product, Agent Auth checks that user's permissions   against the ceiling and only grants the agent  the permissions that show up in both places.  WorkOS does all this with the users  and roles that you've already set up,   so you can give every agent the exact permissions  that it should have without ever needing   to build a separate permission system. Go to workos.com/authkit to learn more.  I think people correctly point out  that I have too many people on my   podcast who have this particular view of AI  trajectories, and not only AI trajectories,   but the implications of that trajectory. However, it does end up being the case   that when you talk to a skeptic, for  example, Ege, it seems like you just   have slightly different probabilities on things. The people who totally dismiss this altogether,   I feel like, don’t have reasonable arguments  about why AI capabilities will not continue.  If you take seriously the possibility of minds  in data centers that learn like humans and   which will swamp us in population, thinking  speed, agglomerated experience and expertise,   et cetera, no people who take that  seriously, at least so far as I’ve found,   put less than 10% or less than 5% that  things go pretty badly for biological humans.  This is something I try to emphasize. By people who don’t have enough context   on the situation, or who are not carefully  reading what I’m saying, I could be considered   this person who disagrees with Daniel, that  I give 2-3x less probability to various   things compared to Daniel or something like that. That’s actually not that important in some sense.  There are some things for which a  3-4x difference can make a difference.  If you think the risk of doom right  now is 4% a year compared to 1% a year,   that can actually make a difference for  whether you think we should pause or not.  That’s because you’re comparing it to  the 1% per year of people who are dying.  Then whether you think the risk per  year from AI is higher or lower than   that is an important analytical question. But compared to the people who just don’t   take the technology seriously, or who have what  I would call magical views about the human mind,   which are very widespread, all of those  people are just in a different world.  They’re not actually engaged  with what’s happening.  If they were making predictions over the past  few years, or past five years or whatever,   they would’ve been very, very, very wrong. All their predictions would’ve been   completely wrong. Often they don’t make   predictions, so they’re not proven wrong. Actually, should we discuss what you,   Daniel, predicted in AI 2027, which  was released in the beginning of 2025?  What did you predict that the  world would look like in late 2026?  The biggest thing that was incorrect was that  we said China wakes up in summer of 2026.  There has been a lot of  wake-up, so to speak, in China.  They’ve started talking a lot more  about existential risk and alignment   and superintelligence and things like that,  but not to the same extent that we predicted.  As far as we know, they haven’t gotten the state  seriously involved in their AI projects and   started funding them more, sharing algorithms  and things like that, and merging compute.  That’s definitely one thing we got wrong. Some of the stuff we got right was relatively   obvious, like the rise of agents, the  rise of coding agents in particular.  For early 2026, the title of our chapter there  was "Coding Automation," which coincided very   nicely with Claude Code taking off. The revenue projections, if anything,   were slightly pessimistic, in the sense that  they were lower than what ended up happening.  But at the same time, by end of year, the market  projections seem like they were too optimistic.  We said 30% or something. Yeah, and if anything, it might   end up being down, or only slightly up. A bunch of AI stocks are down,   Nvidia’s down, and so on. That’s an interesting thing   to also maybe talk about a little bit. To me it looks like there is a big cleavage   in worldviews that’s happening here between people  in finance, people in New York, and people in San   Francisco, maybe is one way to put it. People who are viewing these as just   ordinary stocks see a lot of business risk. They see a lot of default risk on debts.  The business plan doesn’t seem very sustainable. The companies are burning a lot of money.  Even Anthropic still has negative margin, or  maybe very, very slightly positive margin.  So it seems very risky, and they’re like, "Can  this really go on for another one or two years?"  But here people say, "In one or  two years, we might all be dead."  That’s a very big difference in views. Most people in the world, most people who   have a lot of money or whatever, still  don’t believe any of this, basically.  Not only do they not believe  what Daniel is saying, there   is just a general complete skepticism of the  technology, despite what has already happened.  People still don’t, as far as I  can see, just buy this premise.  Humans are physical objects. We have some  capacities. The brain has some capacities.  It’s just a physical object. We have enough resources   to reproduce what it does. Then that’s obviously going to have   completely transformative implications. That argument is very straightforward.  It doesn’t really hinge on these  details about exactly when it happens,   but people just don’t believe it. It seems to me like this very   deep-rooted irrationality that is tied to maybe  lingering notions of the human soul or whatever.  There’s a lot of this going on where people don’t  want to confront the reality of what’s happening.  The basic thing is that there is a massive  transformation that’s going to happen.  And you need to understand it’s going to happen  if you want to talk about, "What do we do?  What do we change? How do we adapt to it? What is our plan?" We have no plan right now.  There’s nothing. The fact that people will be  superseded as the things that produce economic   value, that has dramatic implications. People don’t think that’s going to happen,   so they’re doing nothing about that either. There’s just a bunch of ways in which, with this   transformation of the world, we should  be talking about what we’re going to do.  And we’re not doing that because people  don’t think it’s going to happen.  Not only that, but when you do talk  about it, there’s just a huge backlash.  I think it’s just very psychologically  disturbing to take this possibility seriously.  I released this article about the Hugging  Face incident where I summarized the story.  There was a huge backlash to the fact  that I used the word "civilization"   in it to describe these agent swarms. At the time I thought to myself, "I would   have never guessed that this would have happened. But if I had anticipated it, maybe I could have   just avoided using that word, so people  could actually read what happened and   understand the incident." Then I thought to myself,   "I don’t think it would have mattered. There would have been something else."  You need to find something so you  can’t focus on the story itself.  If you do realize the nature of the story —  forget about the misalignment, just the nature   of the capabilities growth — then one, it’s  just not a comfortable thing to think about.  Two, it makes a lot of other priorities you  might have, a lot of other topics you might   want to focus on instead, much less relevant. With regards to the plan, I’ve been reading these   accounts of what has gone  wrong in wars in the past.  Ege, I know you’ve done a much  deeper dive on these kinds of things.  But why, for example, did World  War I turn into a catastrophe?  Why did America send troops into Vietnam? Why did we do Iraq?  What you find in many of these situations is that  it was not as if the relevant political leaders   got in a room and had a discussion about  the pros and cons, the costs and benefits,   how things could go wrong, for example,  if we invade China, if you’re Japan, or   if you give some security guarantee to Belgium,  or if we send half a million troops into Vietnam:   "What if things escalate in ways we don’t expect? Is that worth the benefits?"  Instead, what has happened in these cases, when  people try to analyze why things went wrong,   is that there actually never was a clear  decision that was made in the first place.  There never was an accounting  of, "This is what could go wrong.  This is what the benefits could be. Do we think it is worth it?"  And often the people who try to make that  discussion happen get socially punished for it.  For example, in Japan, there was a  member of parliament, I forgot his name,   but during the war with China, he stood up in  parliament and was like, "Can someone explain   to me what is the point of this? Why are we in this war?"  Then they kicked him out of parliament. It’s just such an obvious, rational question.  Why are we doing this? What is the point? The motivation,   if you look at that war, for example, was  very religious in many ways. "Japan has   a civilizing mission to save and  liberate East Asia," or whatever.  But what they actually did was totally not that. So it seems like these were not at all decisions   that were rationally made. I agree with you. Often   these things are not planned. Then of course things end up badly.  For the AI thing broadly, what I would  say… There’s this quote from Nietzsche.  He wrote, "God is dead, but given the way of  man, for many thousands of years there may be   caves in which his shadow will be shown,  and we have to vanquish his shadow too."  I think that is what AI is doing. We have all these almost quasi-religious   beliefs about the human mind, and all  of them are going to be undermined.  Some people already realize  God is dead in this sense.  But his shadow is just the things we believe that  are left over from our religious view of humanity.  That’s going to have to go away. Let’s step back. The argument for continuing AI   progress now is that you will get better models. Those better models will help you do security   work, even formally verifying that  your model weights and algorithmic   secrets are extremely safe, rewriting the  entirety of Slack in a safe, secure way.  You will get AIs that are better  at doing alignment research.  You will be doing alignment research on  the models that are closer to the ones   that will actually fully automate AI research. What do you make of the argument that progress   at this pace should continue for three or six more  months, and you then use that crescendo where all   this progress in alignment and security could be  concentrated to make sure that superintelligent   systems have the values we want them to have? Sounds like a really dangerous plan to me.  You could make the argument  in the past, maybe in 2020.  You could say, "We still haven’t figured  out how to turn these things into agents.  So probably whatever alignment techniques  we do on pure predictive language models   aren’t going to generalize or teach us  that much about how to align AI agents."  Well, now we have AI agents. Not only do we have AI agents, but we   are potentially very close to the singularity,  the AI agents that would automate the AI R&D.  It’s like, "Okay, now it’s time to  start slowing down or stopping."  I no longer buy the argument that  our alignment research isn’t that   valuable because our current systems are  just too different from future systems.  They are very different from  superintelligence, that’s for sure.  But they’re not very different from the type  of AI that will potentially pose a threat,   because it’s the type of AI that’s  automating the AI research process.  Therefore, if it’s misaligned, those  misalignments can continue into the future.  Also, if it’s just not doing its job  very well, if it’s more interested in   apparent success than actual success,  then it produces alignment solutions   that don’t actually work but appear to work. Isn’t another way to say what you’re saying that,   even forgetting about the pause, the thing  we need right now more than anything is a   capable alignment researcher, a capable  and trustworthy alignment researcher?  That’s one of the things  that a pause should produce.  I also think that the AIs doing the  intelligence explosion are going to   be under all sorts of external constraints  too, just like today’s current researchers.  Take chain-of-thought monitorability.  This is a classic example of something   where we all agree it would be nice if the  chain of thought were more monitorable.  But also, the things that you would do to make  it more monitorable might make your system more   expensive for a given level of capability,  or less capable at a given level of expense.  The things that you would do to make your system  more capable often make it less monitorable.  There are going to be loads of  trade-offs like that everywhere.  So even if you have managed to succeed in making  an automated alignment researcher that’s genuinely   honest and genuinely cares in a robust way about  doing its job and solving alignment for you,   if you’re doing an intelligence explosion, it’s  going to be facing all these trade-offs where it   has to do the thing that even by its own lights is  a little bit more risky, because it doesn’t have   the compute or the time to do the safer thing. It seems like a big concern of yours with regards   to an intelligence explosion soon is that  you don’t think the ways in which we have   historically made AI systems more aligned, and  are continuing to make AI systems more aligned,   are going to be especially useful for  making superintelligence more aligned.  But if I just think about the things we’re doing  right now, like "Hey, let’s fix the reward hacks.  Let’s make better graders. Let’s make  the gradient of rewards such that the   harder you try to cheat in a way that  you get caught, the more we punish you.  In fact, if you give evidence of your cheating or  you give up early on an impossible task, maybe we   give you the reward you would’ve gotten anyways." AIs are  just derpy and amnesiac, et cetera.  And it’s extreme bullishness on diffusion once  you do have those onboarding capabilities.  I think that’s basically right. My point is not that you can hire   a random person, and a random person can  just use the AI to do a bunch of stuff.  What I’m saying is that the premium to  just having a lot of hands-on experience   with something, especially if it’s in  knowledge work, has gone down a lot.  But the job was that you need to have experience,  and you also need to have these execution skills,   and you need to be generally capable of  making good judgments about various things.  So there are some general skills which are very  valuable, which should become even more valuable,   and finding those people is still hard. So it’s still hard to hire people.  It’s just that you’re hiring them  on a slightly different criterion.  The point I’m making is more narrow,  for what’s happening right now.  A lot of hiring processes were designed for  a time when experience was very important,   and I think that’s no longer true. But the processes are not adapting.  That’s the sort of thing I’m talking about, where  people are in denial, and them being in denial   results in tons of inefficient and bad decisions. As technology advances, the stakes   get higher and higher. That’s why I think it’s   very important for people to have an accurate  assessment of what the technology is capable of.  Predictions for next year. Ege, what do you think  the annualized revenue of the top AI company will   be by the end of next year? Maybe a median estimate of   $250-300 billion a year. What is it right now?  What is Anthropic’s? $90 billion or something like that.  So maybe 2.5-3x bigger than now is my best guess. If you ask me what 2027 looks like, I’ll say,   "Unfortunately, it seems like  it’ll look like AI 2027."  I could be wrong. I’m not confident in that. But it seems to me somewhat more likely than   not that they will have fully automated the AI  research process sometime during the year 2027,   unless they get slowed down by the  government or by voluntary slowdown,   which I do think is substantially possible. I am trying to make it happen that they   slow down and get slowed down. We have a shot. If they don’t   get slowed down, then I think they’ll  fully automate the AI research process.  They’ll get smarter and smarter AIs. How much revenue will they make?  Probably a lot. But it’s also one of these  weird questions where their main consideration   won’t even be revenue at that point. They might even stop serving products   to customers and just use 100% of their  compute for R&D instead of 70% or something.  This was actually one of the  surprising things in the S-1.  In the Anthropic S-1, they said that 70% of their  compute is just going to internal use, which is,   I think, higher than many people expected. It’s already the case that Anthropic is an RSI   company that happens to serve products to users. The other question that’s worth ironing out is:   what is the most capable or impressive thing —  this is a weird question for you, Daniel — that   you expect AI to be able to do by the end of  next year that is not a benchmark, but an actual   realized accomplishment, in the way solving  two Millennium Prize Problems was this year?  Ege, what is the most impressive concrete  accomplishment you expect AI systems to   be able to make by next year? This question is hard to answer   because what is the ordering of impressiveness? For example, one thing I expect is that by the   end of next year, we’ll probably have robots that  can actually do some simple tasks at a reasonable   latency, not where you give the robot two hours  and every action takes two minutes or whatever.  I just expect this because of cost trends. Costs are coming down so dramatically that   you will get small models that are sufficiently  powerful and low latency that you will actually   have robots that look like they can do reasonable,  simple physical things in the real world.  I personally think that would be  very impressive if that happened.  But in the way, for example, that we think  about what would be impressive if a human did   that thing, then of course solving the Riemann  hypothesis is way, way more impressive than   folding laundry in real time or something. But that’s not the way it works for AIs.  It’s also way less economically valuable to solve  the Riemann hypothesis than to be able to do tasks   that are of the form of folding laundry very well. The other thing is that we should expect dramatic   advances in the ability of the  AI systems to do knowledge work.  It’s already starting a little bit. They’re still kind of schleppy and not   amazing at this, but I think they will  get way, way better at computer use.  Next year, you will probably be able to get  systems that can download an arbitrary random   computer game off of Steam and play it the  way that a human would and just complete it.  Not a game they were trained  to play, but an arbitrary game.  Even GTA VI or something? End of 2027, probably yes.  I actually am curious. At the beginning  you said that you expect 15-20 years before   full automation. Of everything.  What do you think will take 15 years? If by the end of 2027 they can do the   arbitrary video games thing and the robots  thing, what’s the remaining 14 years?  When you actually have these robots, it will  feel like having computer use agents right now.  They can do these isolated tasks if  given the instructions to do them.  But if nobody is managing them and constantly  telling them what to do, then they won’t be able   to make autonomous progress on problems. They will not know what to do.  This is what happens right now when  I use the agent swarms, for example.  If I’m not supervising the swarm, then the  swarm just quickly becomes incapable of doing   anything in the real world. They hit blockers. They   don’t know how to resolve them. They miscommunicate. The members of   the swarm lie to each other. They forget information.   It’s surprisingly schleppy. That’s what it  will look like when we have these robots.  It won’t be that we suddenly  have robots and we have this   industrial explosion that suddenly takes off. It will initially be that there are some tasks we   can automate using these models that we couldn’t  do before because our robots were too stupid.  But we won’t get a situation in which  we are getting an industrial explosion,   because there will still be human bottlenecks in  management and telling the systems what to do.  I guess the way we’ve seen automation in  other sectors, it does seem to me that   you get a glimmer of coding ability, and  then you get swamped by coding ability.  It’s not like you get 5% on SWE-bench, and the  year after you get 10%, and then 15%, and 20%,   and then there’s this exponential decrease… That’s not the way I would put it, though.  We have seen a longer tail across skills. What you’re saying is correct for any one   skill that you can measure. But what I just expect is   that there will be more skills of this kind. For example, let’s say you get robots, but they’re   unable to do continual learning or something. That’s probably what happens, actually.  I totally agree with you that if we do the  superintelligence-first thing and then do   the robots, then it will hit us like a truck. But if we instead do robots in the ordinary way,   then for some period of time, they will be  exactly like you describe, where they can   do a specific task if you tell them to. But if you give them a more ambitious,   longer task, like keeping the house clean or  something, then they’ll get stuck or flail around.  But I would apply the concept of horizon lengths  here and say that probably, just like with   many other types of tasks, they would start off  like that, but then the horizon length of tasks   that they can autonomously do would double  twice a year or double three times a year.  Then it seems hard to get 15 years if  that’s what you’re doing, because even   after just the first three years, you’re  getting 100x improvement in horizon length.  So it seems to me that if you think that  by the end of 2027, the AIs will be able   to do dishes or fold laundry when someone  tells them to, then by 2030, they should   be able to just manage the house or something. I’m not sure. The concept of horizon length seems   like too much of a leaky abstraction to me here. When I use agents for coding stuff,   there are tasks which would take a  human many weeks that they can do.  But there are other tasks that would take  a human 10 minutes that they can’t do.  Often it’s not even easy to understand  how these tasks are distributed.  A task can look extremely technically  complicated and ambitious: take this   program and completely formalize it  and prove things about it or whatever.  This is the kind of thing a  human would take many months on.  An agent can often do it in hours. While a much simpler task like,   "I’m going to put you in charge of looking  at other people’s changes to this codebase,   and make sure you don’t approve something if it  looks obviously dumb or if it breaks something,"   this kind of thing, they just can’t retain memory. They can’t understand what it means for something   to be bad or dangerous to merge. It’s because there’s too much context.  They are bad at arranging information in  such a way that they retain all the context,   they know what’s relevant and what’s not relevant. There seems to be something missing there,   and it’s causing their horizon  lengths to be extremely jagged.  On the tasks which are of the second type that  I’m talking about, I don’t think we’ve been seeing   progress that is 10x a year in horizon length. This is a live question for me.  This is something that’s somewhat crux-y for me. If I were more convinced that they were really   not improving that much at a whole  range of really important skills,   that would lengthen my timelines significantly. One question I have is, how much hard evidence   do we have that this is the  case versus just anecdotes?  A skeptical-of-this-hypothesis but more bullish  hypothesis overall about AI would be that,   at any given level of AI capability, there  will still be things that they still can’t do.  As you give your AIs more ambitious  tasks, you’ll still notice that they’re   failing at this sort of thing. You’ll constantly be running   up against their failures. That might give the misleading   impression that they’re not really improving  that much, even if the things that they’re   failing at are more impressive than the  things they were failing at two years ago.  Basically, one thought is, how confident  are you that they really aren’t improving   that much over the years, versus they are  improving a lot, it’s just that there’s a   significant order of magnitude or two gap? It’s difficult to name a task where the   AIs are not making significant  progress, just in capability.  That was not true, I think, some number  of years ago, but right now it is true.  The difference here is more, do you think  the progress in some metric, let’s say   horizon lengths or something like that, is 2-3x  a year, or is it more like 10x or 100x a year?  It’s more a quantitative question as  opposed to, are they making progress or not?  For example, in the skill of writing an original  novel that is good, I think the progress   since last year is definitely not 100x. Probably not even 10x. It might be 3x,   but this is very subjective. It’s very hard to measure this.  But with a lot of these things, we don’t  have anything like METR’s time horizon   benchmark to settle these questions. I’m just having to make these intuitive   judgments because we don’t have good benchmarks. So I could be totally wrong about some of this,   and if you were to quantify it,  it will come out that I was wrong.  With the time horizon thing, I think the issue  is that the moment you turn it into a benchmark,   it has to be something that the AIs can already  do reasonably well enough, that can then become   an optimization target, and that makes it  relatively easy to make progress on it.  My guess of what would happen for the METR  time horizons thing, and I’ve said this,   I think, early last year, was that  this is basically going to diverge.  They’re going to get near infinite time horizon. But there will still be a bunch of just 10-minute   tasks that the AIs can’t actually do very  well because of just distributional shift.  That has basically happened now. They stopped reporting the numbers   because it was diverging. But take some   domain in which they can do a 10-minute task now. What is the length of the task that they will   be able to do in that domain  in one or two or three years?  It’s probably just very domain sensitive. So I don’t really have a very good answer   to this question, because we don’t have  a good benchmark that can settle it.  It’s just my intuitive judgment, based on using  the systems, that they seem like they made vast   progress in math, probably even more than 100x  in terms of time horizon over the last year.  In some other domain — like sending emails  on my behalf that are not confusing and that   people on the other side can understand — I  feel like the progress is much, much less.  I’ll give you a concrete example. For many years, I have been asking any AI CEO who   comes on my podcast how soon before they can  automate being a video editor for my podcast.  The time horizon on that has maybe doubled  over the last year and a half or something.  But if I give Fable a transcript of  my podcast and I’m like, "How should   this be reorganized to be more coherent?" It’s just not clear that there’s been that   much progress from Claude 3.7. Yeah, I think that matches my   qualitative impression. But I thought when I was   using the models that there was a pretty big leap  in, for example, writing quality with 3.6 Sonnet.  It felt like the first model I could actually  use to try to write stories and fiction.  It actually would be decent  if a human was managing it.  In the current state we’re at, they can write  somewhat longer things, but definitely not   100x longer without it becoming bad. I agree, Dwarkesh, that the effective   time horizon, maybe that would be more than 2x  over the last 1.5 years, but it’s not more than   10x over the last 1.5 years. But it’s very subjective.   This is some evidence for the fact that  this rate of progress is incredibly jagged.  In math, since two years ago, it’s  one million times or something.  You can make that case. Some ridiculously high number.  I think this is plausible. My follow-up question then is, to what extent can   this be explained by the training environments? I would imagine that they have a lot of training   environments that are of the form, "Prove this  theorem or disprove this theorem," and a lot of   training environments that are of the form,  "Solve this coding problem," or, "Write this   piece of software that passes these unit tests." And not many problems that are of the form,   "Make a good aesthetic judgment about how  to organize clips" or something like that,   because it’s harder to set up that sort of  environment, and maybe also because it’s less   lucrative, although I’m not sure about that. You work at DeepMind, so do you think that   a lot of this jaggedness is basically  downstream of just the task distribution?  Or do you think that it’s like, "Oh no, I’ve  seen examples of the company trying really   hard to collect a lot of high-quality data and  training environments for a particular type of   10-minute task such as that, and then just  still failing to get the AI as good at it"?  I can’t speak to what the  company is doing internally.  What I can say is based on just public evidence. There’s a cost to verification that I think   is driving a lot of this. I don’t really agree with the   split that some tasks are verifiable  and some tasks are not verifiable.  For example, did you produce a video for  his podcast that will make Dwarkesh happy?  That’s verifiable. You can give the video to  him, and he’s like, "What the hell is that?"  But the issue is that’s a very  expensive way to get feedback.  The difference with math is that math  is very cheap to get feedback on.  There’s a very cheap verifier. That does have a huge effect,   because the way you should think about  it is: how efficiently can you sample   trajectories that give you the right answer? How fast can you discriminate things that   work from those that don’t work? That’s a very fundamental thing for   how efficiently you can learn things. One thing, for example, that makes me   more skeptical of software-only singularity  type stories is that while I agree that ML   research is a verifiable domain, in practice  a lot of the verification is quite expensive.  This is why compute matters so much. That’s why compute is so important   for algorithmic progress. You can have innovations   at small scales that fail at large scales. You can have innovations that only work at large   scales that you can never confirm by experiments  at small scales because they just completely fail.  You get false positives and false  negatives in both directions.  If you want to collect a bunch of data about  this to train the models to have better taste,   that needs a lot of compute as  well, and probably more and more   as you scale up the size of the experiments. That makes me not put as much credit on the   arguments that say, "Look, we made a decade  of progress in one or two months in math,   and therefore we should expect a  decade of progress in ML research."  If you think of the dollar cost of verifying  some idea in ML research and compare it to   the dollar cost of verifying a math proof,  it’s many, many orders of magnitude apart.  Seeing if some proof of the Riemann  hypothesis in Lean is correct or not,   you can do that on your personal computer. It’s very easy. There’s a linear time   algorithm for checking proofs, basically. While if you’re trying to figure out, "I have this   fancy change to this optimizer, does that really  give me a compute efficiency when I’m pre-training   or not?", it’s very hard to settle that question. You can do small-scale experiments.  It can look like it works, but then you  scale it up and, "Oh wait, it doesn’t work.  What’s going on?" Then it’s very confusing.  To me, it looks like the cost of verification   is much, much higher. That’s probably, honestly,   a key reason to expect that domain to be  significantly more difficult to automate.  It’s not that humans are very good at it, because  I think humans are also bad at ML research,   just like we’re bad at math. It’s just that AIs,   due to their current sample inefficiency and  stuff like that, really benefit from being   able to get just a ton of data in there. That is very contingent on there being a   very cheap verification procedure for  whether you did the right thing or not.  The more expensive that is, the  slower you make progress, basically.  So that’s my rough take about this. There is some argument about   generalization with respect to the cost. Even in math, presumably the way that   these models became good at, say,  being able to accommodate billions   of tokens — or was it hundreds of millions of  tokens — in order to solve Navier-Stokes across   a swarm of thousands of agents was not through  many other tasks where 1,000 agents collaborated   in order to solve a math proof and spent tens of  millions of dollars’ worth of tokens to do so.  There was some generalization to a much  more ambitious kind of assignment from   the math training that they underwent. Then the question is, will you see that   kind of generalization in AI research? Now, of course, they’re much more   sample efficient than humans, so you  can’t use this as an exact analogy.  But my understanding is that researchers  who were in the field in, say, 2020,   when there was much less compute being used, at a  level of compute that can be part of the training   process now, are good at doing AI research now. There are some lessons they learned from training   GPT-2- or GPT-3-size models that are helping  them do good research at the current frontier.  So it does seem like you should expect  to see this kind of generalization.  I agree that you could not cheaply and  consistently verify at the scale at which   you’d need the AI researchers operating. I totally agree with that.  You should expect to see a lot of generalization. In fact, we have seen a lot of generalization,   as you said, just based on Navier-Stokes. The other thing I would say is that   there is such a thing as general intelligence. With these base models, I think pre-training   loss is a pretty good proxy for that thing. It does just predict, in a bunch of ways,   "Will the model understand some subtlety  about your request and interpret it correctly   even though it was ambiguous?" and all kinds of  things we normally associate with intelligence.  It just does predict it. Obviously the entire reason this field   works at all is because this concept exists. Otherwise this wouldn’t work.   I totally agree with that. For example, there was this plot   that was published by Anthropic about pre-training  compute multiplier sizes or something like that.  They didn’t report actual sizes, but there  was a plot published in their IPO roadshow.  I have some difficulty interpreting that plot. I can’t exactly say what I think is wrong with it.  I think they’re not disclosing a lot  of information that is relevant for   thinking about whether you trust their  judgment of what’s going on or not.  I can say, based on the information I have,  that I don’t trust their judgment of what’s   going on, but I can’t explain why. That’s a little bit unsatisfying.  Does that mean you think that there hasn’t  been an acceleration in pre-training   progress over the last year at Anthropic? I would say that question is poorly posed.  I don’t think I can elaborate more  than that without revealing something.  You can say there has been and there hasn’t. It depends on how you interpret the question.  Interesting. I’ll put that in  Claude and see what it thinks.  It’s an update to hear that you don’t believe it.  So that’s something. I’m not saying I don’t believe it.  I’m saying the thing they are  reporting is poorly posed.  I’m not saying they made up the numbers. I think there is a real graph inside   Anthropic that probably looks like that. They didn’t fabricate the numbers.  It’s just that I think that doesn’t mean  what they are portraying it to mean.  I’m guessing what you’re referring to  is that there’s some synthetic-data-type   compute multiplier that makes it look  like the loss on that corpus is higher,   but maybe in a way that doesn’t generalize. Of course, I can only speculate, but these   are the kinds of things one could think  make the pre-training thing misleading.  I can’t comment on that. But this is a trade-off.  This is something people have to decide. You can decide people should be more transparent.  You can have a regulation that  companies have to be more transparent,   they have to publish a bunch of information. But then you have to accept the fact that anything   that is published, China also finds out. Well, China’s finding out anyways.  At least we get to find out. Yeah, I accept that fact.  They’re probably finding out anyway. Right now, there’s a lot of leakage   because security posture is so bad. But in a world where you also want to   improve the security posture, doing both  of these interventions at once defeats a   lot of the point of improving security, if  you’re also going to get the labs to publish   all of this information anyway. Maybe you can defend the weights,   and the weights are not going to get stolen. But basically everything else, all the algorithmic   innovations and so on, they would very easily  just reconstruct from the public information.  That is a cost. It might be a cost worth  paying, depending on how dire you think the   situation is in a bunch of ways. I think it is worth paying.  But then the proper way to do that… Again,  that’s why I think improving the quality of   public discourse, not about these specific  details, but just about the general fact of   the transformativeness of the technology and the  size of the impact it will have, is so important.  If the public takes this seriously, then this is  a decision that could be made by the government.  Then it could become a regulation. We could just accept that, "Yes, we understand   there’s a cost here, but given the stakes of the  situation, we think we should pay this cost."  For example, Anthropic doesn’t believe that. Even though they also are aware of the stakes,   they just don’t think that cost is worth paying. I think that’s what’s going on.  I don’t think they’re necessarily  being self-interested about that.  They just have a real belief that  this would be worse for the world   if they made that information public. But Daniel doesn’t share that belief.  If there’s no public discourse about it,  it’s impossible to get the companies to   actually publish this stuff. There has to be some external   thing that comes in and says, "Look, you guys can  think that, but we are aware of the stakes here.  We have decided that it is important  for this information to be public."  Unless that can happen, anyone can say,  "Look, I think it’s better for the world,   and I’m just going to do what I think is best." There’s no regulation, there are no rules.  That’s a very bad situation. Not because I necessarily think that the decision   to keep it secret is a wrong decision, but because  the process that’s outputting that outcome is bad.  As I said, there should be a plan. We should understand what the stakes are.  There should be rational public  deliberation about this topic,   and people should come to a conclusion: "Yes,  we want this," or, "No, we don’t want this."  That has not happened at all. This is a unilateral decision that is being taken   by some people who might be right, might be wrong. They have certain preferences. Even the   government, I think, is not really  playing a large role in that,   because they don’t understand the stakes. The government might play a role in something   like, "Oh, we are worried about Chinese cyber  attacks, and we want to have capable cyber models.  We don’t want that to get leaked." Or they might worry about specific concrete risks.  But if you don’t appreciate the total  transformative potential of the technology,   that it’s going to totally change  the human condition, for example,   then you’re just unaware of the stakes. You’re not going to make the right decisions.  This was a very productive discussion. I feel it was very helpful to iron out what   the cruxes were within the context of people who  take the potential of this technology seriously.  Thanks, guys. Thank you.

transcript_segments.text: Today, I’m joined by Ege  Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo.
Ege is a researcher at Google DeepMind. Daniel is one of the authors at the AI Futures
Project, which published AI 2027 and AI 2040. I wouldn’t call this exactly a debate,
because I hope it’ll be more of a discussion. But there is a set of key disagreements you
guys have, which leads one of you, Daniel,  to believe that AI is likely to kill us all
within the next few years, and Ege,  you to believe that will not happen.
I feel like a big crux in this  conversation is just timelines.
How soon do you expect extreme superintelligence? I’ve articulated, and Paul has articulated in
the last episode, why there could  be extreme superintelligence soon.
Ege, why do you think that’s unlikely? The main difference between me and Daniel,
and also between me and Paul, is just how much  you believe in the software-only singularity.
This is the idea that you have a fixed  pool of compute and a roughly fixed
amount of data that is at least not synthetic. Then what happens is that you get better AIs.
Those AIs are able to use that pool of  resources way more efficiently to make
progress on AI research, and you get this  feedback loop that at least goes for many
orders of magnitude before it fizzles out. Then that improvement is so big that you get,
I don’t know, 10 years of progress in six  months or whatever, something like this.
I think the evidence we have is not  sufficient to give high credence to that.
Maybe that’s 10-20% likely to  happen over the next three years.
That’s probably the biggest disagreement,  where Daniel thinks that’s over 50% likely.
Why do you think it’s more than 50% likely  that there will be extreme superintelligence
within the next few years, whereas  Ege thinks that’s 10-20% likely?
First of all, I don’t think that we will  probably all be dead in a couple years.
The thing I would say is, unless we substantially  slow down the AI companies, then probably we will
lose control and there will be misaligned  AIs running the show in a couple years.
It seems like we’re getting close to  fully automating the AI research process.
That would be the main claim. How close? It seems like
it’s going to happen in 2027. Maybe not, maybe 2028, maybe 2029, but I would
say it’s slightly more likely than not in 2027. Once you have fully automated the AI research
process, things will probably accelerate. More likely than not, they will accelerate a lot,
as Ege was describing, although I do  think there’s some uncertainty there.
Then I think that a lot of the limitations of  current AI systems, such as the data inefficiency
or whatever, will melt away relatively  quickly as progress accelerates dramatically.
You’ll end up with AIs that are able to flexibly  learn quickly from all sorts of experience.
You might call them  top-expert-dominating AIs, perhaps.
Top-expert-dominating AIs are effectively  superintelligence as far as I’m concerned.
Here’s a naive question. We go back five  years and we have AI systems that can’t
even hold a conversation. Now we have systems that
are solving Millennium Prize Problems. They’re pretty good coders, et cetera.
If we just go another five years of  progress at this pace, do you think
it’s likely that that alone gives us AIs  that are competitive with human experts?
If we’re looking forward five years,  do we even need that much RSI?
We might not, but I think it’s unclear. If we don’t get any RSI, my median timeline
to everything being automated and humans having  nothing to do — they’ve been completely automated
— is something like 15-20 years from now. That’s a median timeline. So in the next
five years, you still have to give it  20% or something that it could happen.
I think that’s a very live possibility. While there are disagreements about software-only
singularity and similar things, in some sense  those disagreements don’t matter that much.
All I’m saying is, Daniel is saying something is  50-60% likely to happen over the next three years,
and I’m saying it’s 20% likely. That question might be interesting.
But even if it’s only 20% likely,  if the situation is very bad,
you should still do something about it. So even though it’s maybe a larger
disagreement numerically, I don’t think it’s  a significant disagreement qualitatively.
So the reason why you’re working at Google  instead of protesting outside of Anthropic,
which is a practical difference between our  behavior, is less to do with the probabilities
on the different scenarios and more to do  with… Well, what actually? I’m curious.
Several things. In this particular question  of whether a pause is a good idea or not,
I’m worried about any plan that involves us acting  on risks before we have seen some significant
version of the costs in the real world. Right now, the thing people always cite
in these discussions, since some number of  months ago, is the Hugging Face incident.
But I personally think the Hugging Face incident  didn’t cost that much and was a pretty small
incident in the grand scheme of things. It was much less significant than a plane
crash in terms of the cost imposed. I do see it as analogous to if you
have a new technology, like nuclear  reactors or aircraft or whatever,
